Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/3/Text/7] Then two unconditional growth models were estimated using different time metrics of changes in life satisfaction; chronological age; and time-to- [/page/4/Text/7] death. In both the age-based model (-.32, SE = .07, p\.001) and in the time-to-death model (-.39, SE = .07, p\.001) there were significant linear declines in life satisfaction. No fixed or random quadratic slope effects were found significant. [/page/4/Text/8] Table 2 presents the results from two estimated time-todeath models. Model A1 including gender, age, SES, yearsto-death at wave 1, and overall load of disease as covariates and show that less overall load of disease was significantly related to higher levels of life satisfaction (.49, SE = .11, p\.001).
